newsitem.title: FINLAND: Russian copper concentrate output to mark time.
newsitem.headline: Russian copper concentrate output to mark time.

text.p: Russian output of copper concentrate is unlikely to expand much in the near term as better results at big producers will be counteracted by declines in smaller operations, delegates at the Metal Bulletin Base Metal Concentrate conference were told on Thursday.

The top six producers in the former Soviet Union -- including Norilsk in Russia, Zhezkazghanstvetmet in Kazakhstan and Almalyk in Uzbekistan -- accounted for 77 percent of the total production last year, said analyst James May of Metal Bulletin Research.

On the plus side, metal giant Norilsk will remain a significant producer of copper although its focus is primarily nickel and it appears unlikely that copper-in-concentrate will become a commodity product, he said.
Production at Russia's Urals-based copper producers is just 30,000 tonnes below its 1989 peak and Kazakhstan's industry is benefitting from foreign investment.
But the remaining 22 facilities saw their combined output falling nearly 40 percent, compared to 15 percent for the largest operations.
Smaller operations are becoming unviable because of high transport costs, lack of working capital or adequate reserves for economic mining, he said.
The majority of mines in the former Soviet Union produce less than 10,000 tonnes per year and a significant fall in the copper price could spell bankruptcy for some of them.

Any tightning of concentrate supply will also hurt the ability of smelters to source their concentrates locally. Increasingly feed for refiners and smelters has come from scrap, which has affected quality of output.
Economic operations are looking towards vertical and horizontal integration to guarantee raw materials, find end use markets for their products and to reduce costs, he said.

"This is rather ironic given the incredible amount of political will that was spent breaking up the integrated structures of the Soviet-era industry....but it also reflects the ability of the market to make decisions about production," he said.
Smelters having difficulty sourcing raw material domestically their raw material are unlikely to find tolling a substantial alternative.
"The build up in concentrates over the last few years -- the so-called 'smelter bottleneck' is likely to disappear over the next two years," May said.
The level of concentrates imports will also depend on whether smelters will be able to afford them.

"Assuming that the smelting sector continues to be relatively successful, there is likely to be a slight increase in the level of imports of concentrate from the West, although the tightening of the global concentrate market in the next few years is likely to limit any expansion," May said.
